title: I Have Loved You: Contempt at the Altar
summary: The LORD declares his love for Israel and, when the people ask for proof, points to his choice of Jacob over Esau and the ruin of Edom. He then turns on the priests, who despise his name by offering blind, lame, and sick animals they would never dare give their governor. God would rather the temple doors were shut, for his name will be great among the nations, from sunrise to sunset.
story: The exiles have been home for decades. Under Haggai and Zechariah they rebuilt the temple, finished in 515 BC, and restarted the sacrifices, expecting that God's glory would fill the house and the nations would stream to Jerusalem. It did not happen the way they had pictured. Judah remains a small, poor province of the Persian Empire, and a slow cynicism has set in, first among the priests. Malachi opens his book not with a rebuke but with a declaration of love, and then shows what the people's worship reveals about their view of God. The contempt exposed in this chapter will spread in chapter 2 to the priests' teaching and to the people's marriages.
historical:
The book is usually dated to the middle of the fifth century BC, around the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. Verse 8 mentions the governor, the Persian-era official who ruled Judah on behalf of the king; Nehemiah held that office from 445 BC, and Nehemiah 5:14-15 speaks of governors before him who burdened the people. A priest who would not dare present a sick animal as a gift to such a man was presenting it to God.

Edom, the people descended from Esau, lived southeast of the Dead Sea. The two nations had a long, bitter history, and Edom was remembered for gloating and joining in when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC (Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10-14). In the century that followed, Edom's own land was devastated, and Arab peoples, later known as the Nabataeans, gradually moved into its territory while many Edomites were pushed west into southern Judah. By Malachi's day Edom's heartland lay in ruins, which is the evidence God points to in verses 3 and 4.
cultural:
The law of Moses required that animals offered to God be without defect (Leviticus 22:17-25; Deuteronomy 15:21). A sacrifice was a gift from the worshiper's own flock, and a blemished animal said that God deserved leftovers. The table of the LORD in verses 7 and 12 is the altar, pictured as the place where God receives the food of his people's gifts; parts of many offerings also fed the priests, which makes their complaint that the food is contemptible all the more telling. The phrase What a nuisance, and the gesture of turning up one's nose, capture bored professionals who have come to resent their work.

The language of father and master in verse 6 drew on the basic honor codes of the ancient world. A son owed honor to his father and a servant owed respect to his master, and failure to show it was shameful. God asks only for what any household head would expect. The vow of verse 14 was a common practice, a promise to give God a particular animal in return for help, and substituting a worse one afterward was a kind of fraud.
literary: Malachi 1 contains the first two of the book's six disputations. Each follows the same pattern: God makes a statement, the people object with a question introduced by but you ask, and God answers with evidence. The first (verses 2 to 5) is short and turns on the pair loved and hated. The second (1:6 to 2:9) is longer; this chapter gives its indictment and chapter 2 gives the sentence. The repetition of My name, which returns again and again in the chapter, carries the argument: the priests who should guard God's name despise it, while the nations will make it great. The refrain says the LORD of Hosts, repeated again and again, keeps reminding the reader who is speaking and how much greater he is than any governor.

outline.t: Heading: the burden of the LORD through Malachi
The first dispute: God's love for Jacob and judgment on Edom
The priests despise God's name with defiled offerings
God's name great among the nations
Contempt for the altar and the curse on the cheat

doctrines.note: God's opening word is love, and it is covenant love, grounded in his choice of Jacob rather than in Israel's merit. Every rebuke that follows assumes that relationship.
Worship reveals what worshipers believe about God. Offering him defective animals treats the holy God as less worthy than a Persian official, and God rejects worship that holds him in contempt.
Verse 11 looks beyond Israel: God's name will be great among the nations, with pure offerings in every place. The failure of Israel's priests does not limit God's purpose to be known everywhere.

words.note: Ahav, to love. The book's first word from God is I have loved you. The verb covers affection, friendship, and covenant loyalty, and in treaties of the ancient Near East love could describe a king's faithful commitment to a vassal. God's love here is his settled, choosing commitment to Israel.

Sane, to hate. Set beside love, it often expresses choice or preference rather than emotional loathing: Jacob loved Rachel and Leah was hated, meaning loved less (Genesis 29:30-31), and Deuteronomy 21:15 speaks of a loved and an unloved wife. In verse 3 it speaks of Esau not chosen and Edom under judgment.

Bazah, to despise or treat as worthless. Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:34), and now the priests despise God's name. The word describes not open hatred but contempt: treating something precious as if it did not matter.

Minchah, offering or gift. It can mean the grain offering of Leviticus 2 or any gift offered as tribute. In verses 10, 11, and 13 it is the broad word for what worshipers bring, and verse 11 promises a pure minchah among the nations.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ is thematic rather than predictive. Malachi's complaint is that worship has become empty and grudging, and Jesus would later confront the same thing in the temple of his own day, quoting Isaiah and Jeremiah as he drove out the traders (Matthew 21:12-13). Verse 11 promises pure offerings to God's name in every place among the nations. The New Testament describes the worship of the church in those terms: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, not tied to one mountain (John 4:21-24), and Hebrews calls believers to offer a sacrifice of praise through Christ (Hebrews 13:15). Early Christians, as in the Didache (an early church manual usually dated to the late first or early second century), applied verse 11 to the church's worship. Behind it all stands Christ's own offering, which Hebrews presents as the one sacrifice truly without blemish (Hebrews 9:14).

hard.q: What does it mean that God loved Jacob and hated Esau, and how does Paul use it in Romans 9?
hard.a:
In Malachi the pair refers first to nations, Israel and Edom, and to God's choice of Jacob's line to carry the covenant. The language of love and hate often expresses choosing and not choosing in Hebrew (compare Genesis 29:30-31), and the evidence Malachi gives is historical: Edom's land lies in ruins while Israel has been brought back. It is not a statement of God's feelings toward Esau as a person, and Genesis itself shows God blessing Esau with land and descendants (Genesis 33 and 36).

Paul quotes the line in Romans 9:13 to argue that God's promises have never depended on human descent or effort but on his free choosing. How far Paul's argument extends is debated. Reformed interpreters read Romans 9 as teaching God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation. Many Arminian and other interpreters read it as God's choice of peoples and roles in the story of redemption, pointing out that Malachi speaks of nations. Both agree that God's election is gracious, never earned, and that Malachi's point is the assurance of his love to a doubting people.

questions: The people ask God how he has loved them. What circumstances make you ask that question, and what evidence would Malachi point you to?
The priests would never give their governor what they gave God. Where do you give God your leftovers of time, attention, or money?
Verse 13 captures worship that has become a nuisance. What helps renew a sense of wonder when faith has become routine?
